title: Anthropic Interviews No Longer Include Handwritten Coding: In the AI Era, Engineers' Value Is Now Weighed by Actual Impact

content_html:
Have candidates write code by hand, only to see otherwise strong performers fail—so Anthropic simply changed the test. According to a Nov. 27 report by Business Insider, platform engineering lead Katelyn Less revealed that the team is experimenting with a new interview format: in addition to traditional programming ability, it will assess whether candidates can use coding agents to do real work, such as reviewing code written by an agent and collaborating with it to build systems.

New interview questions—and new promotion yardsticks

The change came from an awkward discovery: some candidates performed excellently in other stages but stumbled on handwritten code. Less called this “a major shift,” and the team is still looking for the best way to assess whether someone can skillfully use these tools to get work done.

AI is also rewriting promotion criteria. She noted that work that used to take years can now be completed in months, so judging whether someone is qualified for promotion purely by how long a project takes is far less useful than it once was; her team focuses more on tangible outcomes such as reducing system latency and preventing incidents—“Ultimately, it comes down to actual impact.” The higher the level, the more the problem domains and systems each person is responsible for differ, so the company continually adjusts its evaluation methods to measure the complexity of each person’s work.

The share of coding will shrink noticeably

In Less’s view, as agents accelerate development, the way engineers create value is changing: the focus is shifting from writing code to “orchestration”—both getting team members and agents to work together effectively and knowing how to turn an idea into a high-quality product release. Her summary is blunt: “The implementation part will account for a much smaller share—very noticeably smaller.”

This challenge isn’t Anthropic’s alone: as AI drastically compresses the time needed to complete complex work, every manager must answer anew how to evaluate employees’ expertise, career growth, and promotion eligibility.
